subject: English
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 12 periods = 480 minutes
Total: 12 periods · 8h 0min

periods.activity_title: Stepping into the Absurd World of the Funny Man

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us read (p.59): pre-reading activation — things that make us laugh.

time_bands.activity: Invite students to look around and recall things or people that make them laugh. Take two or three quick responses aloud to warm the room.
Read the full poem “A Funny Man” aloud, teacher modelling expression; students follow in their books (p.59–60). Pause after each stanza to let the image settle.
Return to the pre-reading bubbles task from “Let us read” (p.59): students share what struck them as funny or surprising in the poem, building a brief class list on the board.

periods.teacher_notes: The poem's central comic device is physical inversion — shoe on head, hats on feet — paired with impeccable courtesy; keep the read-aloud playful so students feel the absurdist tone before analysis begins. The word ‘funny’ is deliberately paired with the wrong sense word in each stanza (sounding sight, feeling sound), so flag this as something to watch for rather than explain it now. Students who read a different poem or no poem at home can still participate fully since the text is read in class.

periods.activity_title: True, False and the Funny Man — First Comprehension Check

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us discuss (p.61): identify true statements about the funny man — pairs.
Let us discuss (p.61): identify poem words from given meanings — currant, staggered.

time_bands.activity: Quick recap: teacher reads two lines from the poem and asks students to say in one word what the funny man was doing — activating the poem's imagery before comprehension work.
Pairs work through the six statements in “Let us discuss” (p.61), ticking those they believe are true; teacher circulates, then whole-class verification with reasoning drawn from the poem.
Word-hunt from “Let us discuss” (p.61): students decode the two gapped words (currant bun, staggered) using the letter scaffolds given, then say each in a sentence to confirm meaning.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often mark statement 5 (funny man gave a rose) as true because the man announces a rose — but he produces a currant bun; emphasise the gap between what is said and what is done as a key absurdist move in the poem. Statement 2 (ill-mannered) is a common trap: the poem is explicit that his manners were polite. The word ‘staggered’ may be unfamiliar; contextual guessing from the letter scaffold is the intended skill.

periods.activity_title: Tone, Rhyme and the Poet's Craft

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us discuss (p.61): complete sentences — tone, rhyme scheme, repetition of ‘funny’.
Let us discuss (p.61): choose correct answer — imagery, structure, alliteration.

time_bands.activity: Teacher writes ABCB on the board and asks students to map it onto stanza 1 of the poem, confirming the rhyme scheme together before the task.
Students complete the three sentence-frames in “Let us discuss” (p.61) on tone, rhyme scheme and the repetition of ‘funny’; pairs compare before whole-class discussion.
Work through the three bracket-choice questions in “Let us discuss” (p.61) — imagery, monologue-vs-dialogue structure, and alliteration — as a guided class conversation with textual evidence.

periods.teacher_notes: The poem's ABCB rhyme scheme gives each stanza a bouncy, song-like quality; let students tap the rhythm lightly to feel the bounce before labelling it. The dialogue structure (stanzas 3, 4 and 6 contain speech) is often missed because students conflate ‘dialogue’ with a play format — the presence of quoted speech is the marker. The synesthetic oxymorons (‘sounding sight’, ‘feeling sound’) will come up again in the next section; briefly flag that these will be explored more closely.

periods.activity_title: Inversion and Synesthesia — Close Reading of Extracts

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us discuss (p.61–62): rewrite inverted lines; explain synesthetic phrases.
Let us think and reflect (p.62): extract 1 — ‘Your Highness’, polite phrase, currant bun, ‘Well!’

time_bands.activity: Students rewrite the inverted couplet from “Let us discuss” (p.61) in natural word order, then discuss why the poet used phrases like ‘funny sounding sight’ and ‘funny feeling sound’ — pairs first, then share.

Guided close reading of Extract 1 from “Let us think and reflect” (p.62): teacher reads the extract aloud, then class works through all four sub-questions — address of ‘Your Highness’, polite phrase, currant bun identification, and the meaning of ‘Well!’ — as teacher-led discussion with individual written responses.

periods.teacher_notes: The address ‘Your Highness’ is part of the funny man’s consistent exaggerated courtesy; students sometimes read it as mockery — steer them toward seeing it as absurdist politeness consistent with his entire character. The synesthetic phrases mix sensory channels deliberately (sight + sound, feeling + sound); it helps to ask which sense the word properly belongs to, then which sense the poem pairs it with. Students who find the inverted syntax challenging can try reading it aloud with natural stress before rewriting.

periods.activity_title: The Final Twist — Extract 2 and Reflective Questions

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think and reflect (p.63): extract 2 — unique sound, ‘my friend’, reaction, mood.
Let us think and reflect (p.63): reflective questions — mood, alternative title, dialogues.

homework.task_brief: Let us think and reflect (p.62): real-world situations with similar absurd behaviour — brief written note.

time_bands.activity: Students work through Extract 2 from “Let us think and reflect” (p.63): identify the line indicating unique sound, complete the gap on ‘my friend’, explain the funny man’s reaction, and choose the mood of the final line — written individually, then compared with a partner.

Whole-class discussion on three reflective questions from “Let us think and reflect” (p.63): how the unusual behaviour shapes the poem’s mood, an alternative title with reasons, and why the poet chose to include dialogues — teacher scribes key ideas on the board.

periods.teacher_notes: The funny man’s non-answer (hopping home on his head instead of replying) is the poem’s best joke and its thesis: his world is permanently inverted, and he owes no explanation; help students see the ending as confirmation rather than evasion. The mood question often generates varied responses — ‘cheerful’ and ‘dreamy’ are both defensible; ask students to point to specific words that support their choice. The homework task on real-world absurd behaviour (clowns, street performers) connects the poem to lived experience without requiring any previous class activity.

periods.activity_title: Listening to a Funny Mix-Up — Sequencing a Personal Anecdote

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us listen (p.65): select the picture related to the girl’s narration.
Let us listen (p.66): arrange seven events in order of occurrence.

time_bands.activity: Brief orientation: teacher tells students they will hear a girl describe a funny, absent-minded mix-up; ask them to listen for what she did wrong. Students look at the four pictures on p.65 before listening.
Teacher reads the listening transcript aloud at a moderate pace (first listening); students individually circle or note the picture from “Let us listen” (p.65) they believe matches the narration.
Teacher reads the transcript a second time; students now arrange the seven events in order of occurrence using the table in “Let us listen” (p.66). Pairs compare their sequences.
Whole-class verification of both tasks: correct picture identification and event sequence confirmed against the transcript; brief discussion on why absent-minded mistakes strike us as funny.

periods.teacher_notes: The transcript describes a girl so preoccupied with a presentation that she puts her plate on her desk and her shoes in the kitchen — an inversion that echoes the poem’s own upside-down logic; a brief link to the funny man’s world enriches the discussion. The sequencing task requires careful attention to the order of actions (shoes removed first, then eating, then the mix-up); students who struggle should be directed to the causal chain rather than random trial. The transcript is on p.88 of the textbook and must be read by the teacher rather than played from a device unless a recording is available.

periods.activity_title: Telling Jokes Aloud — Voice, Timing and Pair Performance

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us speak (p.66): read and perform the man-and-God joke in pairs with correct voices.
Let us speak (p.66): create and perform an original joke in pairs before the class.

time_bands.activity: Teacher models the man-and-God joke from “Let us speak” (p.66) alone, showing how a flat voice for the narrator, a respectful voice for the man, and a deep voice for God change the comedy. Students mark the voice cues in their books.
Pairs rehearse the joke, taking turns in each role; teacher circulates and coaches timing and volume. One or two pairs perform for the class and receive brief feedback on voice differentiation.

Pairs brainstorm and agree on a simple original joke following a similar three-turn structure from “Let us speak” (p.66), then perform it in front of the class; audience listens for the punchline and responds.

periods.teacher_notes: The humour of the man-and-God joke rests entirely on the double meaning of ‘a minute’ and ‘a rupee’ in God’s frame; pairs who rush through the lines miss the pause that lets the punchline land — a slow delivery after the last request is the key. Some students may feel shy about performing; pairing a confident speaker with a hesitant one and assigning clear roles (narrator vs. character) helps. Original jokes need only a simple two-character exchange with a twist; do not set a length expectation.

periods.activity_title: Writing a Limerick — AABBA and the Art of the Unexpected Ending

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us write (p.66–67): study example limericks, identify rhyme scheme, write an original limerick.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the two example limericks from “Let us write” (p.66) aloud with exaggerated rhythm; students mark the end-rhymes and confirm the AABBA scheme together, noting which lines rhyme and which are shorter.

Guided class construction of one shared limerick on the board using the template on p.67 — teacher invites contributions line by line, discussing how to keep the rhythm bouncy and the ending unexpected.

Students write their own original limericks independently using the template from “Let us write” (p.67); teacher circulates, prompts stuck students with a place name or character to start, and brief peer sharing at the end.

periods.teacher_notes: The most common stumbling block is lines 3 and 4 — students often make them too long and lose the shorter, faster rhythm that lines 3–4 of a limerick require; remind them that these two lines should feel like a quick pair. The unexpected final line is the punchline, so it needs to connect back to line 1 with a twist, not just rhyme with it. Students may write in any voice or setting; the only non-negotiable is the AABBA rhyme and the five-line structure.

periods.activity_title: Phrasal Verbs with TAKE — Meaning, Match and Use

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn (p.64): match five TAKE phrasal verbs to their meanings.
Let us learn (p.64): fill blanks with correct TAKE phrasal verb, adjusting tense.

time_bands.activity: Teacher writes the three poem phrases — ‘walking down’, ‘taking out’, ‘sat down’ — on the board and asks students what each verb + particle pair means together; establish that a phrasal verb’s meaning is often not predictable from its parts alone.
Students match the five TAKE phrasal verbs to their meanings in “Let us learn” (p.64); pairs check each other, then teacher reveals and discusses any contested matches with contextual examples.

Students complete the five fill-in-the-blank sentences from “Let us learn” (p.64), adjusting tense where needed; teacher circulates and highlights tense-change decisions (e.g. ‘took off’ vs. ‘take off’) before whole-class review.

periods.teacher_notes: Students regularly confuse ‘take in’ (comprehend) with ‘take up’ (begin a hobby) — both involve accepting something, so the difference lies in whether the object is abstract knowledge or an activity; a quick sentence contrast on the board helps. The tense-change requirement in the fill-in task is deliberate: sentence 4 (‘the smartphone quickly ___ the sales’) requires the simple past ‘took off’, not the base form. The poem itself uses phrasal verbs naturally, so returning to ‘walking down’ or ‘taking out’ in context anchors the grammar in a familiar text.

periods.activity_title: Building More Phrasal Verbs and a Scale of Movement

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn (p.64): match verbs (look, run, put, break, call) with particles; write meanings.
Let us learn (p.65): arrange movement words in increasing pace order.

homework.task_brief: Let us learn (p.65): frame five original sentences using any five phrasal verbs studied.

time_bands.activity: Students pair the five verbs (look, run, put, break, call) with suitable particles from the given list and write meanings in Column 3 of “Let us learn” (p.64); pairs share their combinations, noting that multiple correct answers are possible and the class builds a collective list.

Teacher writes the movement words from “Let us learn” (p.65) — stagger, walk, hop, run and the three to place — on the board; students arrange them in increasing pace order, discuss their reasoning, and connect stagger and hop back to the funny man in the poem.

periods.teacher_notes: The verb-plus-particle task has many valid combinations (e.g. ‘look after’, ‘look for’, ‘look into’ are all correct for ‘look’); accept all contextually plausible pairings and focus class energy on accuracy of the meaning written, not on finding one right answer. The pace scale (stagger → walk → jog → hop → trot → run → sprint) may generate disagreement about whether trot is faster than jog; treat this as productive discussion rather than a single-answer exercise. The homework sentence-writing task is self-contained and requires no materials beyond the phrasal verbs studied in class.

periods.activity_title: Wit and Wisdom — Humorous Characters Across Indian Traditions

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us explore (p.67): read and share a story featuring Tenali Rama, Birbal, Mullah Nasruddin or Betal.
Let us explore (p.68): share a humorous or nonsense poem from a native language; explain its comedy.

time_bands.activity: Teacher briefly names the four wit-and-humour characters from “Let us explore” (p.67) — Tenali Rama, Birbal, Mullah Nasruddin, King Vikramaditya and Betal — and asks if anyone knows a story involving any of them; one or two quick responses.

Students take a few minutes to recall or read a short story from memory or from available library/textbook material, then share in small groups; two or three groups share with the class, the teacher drawing out what makes the humour work (wit, reversal, unexpected logic).

Students share a funny or nonsense poem from their own language from “Let us explore” (p.68), explaining in brief what makes it funny; teacher connects shared examples to the absurdist inversion at the heart of “A Funny Man” and mentions Sukumar Ray’s Abol Tabol as a bridge.

periods.teacher_notes: Students who cannot recall a specific story should be encouraged to describe any humorous folktale character they know — the sharing is the learning, and no prepared text is required. The connection to Sukumar Ray and Abol Tabol is particularly strong because his nonsense poetry in Bengali uses the same inversion logic as Natalie Joan’s poem; if any student knows a Ray poem, that is worth a moment. Native-language poems need not be translated formally — a brief explanation of the joke or image is enough.
materials: Library books or available folktale collections (optional)

periods.activity_title: The Upside-Down World — A Chapter-Wide Synthesis

time_bands.activity: Teacher leads a swift whole-poem revisit: reads two stanzas aloud and asks students to name every inversion they can spot — physical, linguistic and sensory — building a class list on the board.

Students write a short paragraph (four to six sentences) in which they explain what the funny man’s world reveals about the power of inversion in poetry, using at least one phrasal verb and one example of the ABCB rhyme scheme in their explanation.

Pairs share their paragraphs and give one piece of feedback: does the paragraph name a specific line from the poem and a specific grammar concept? Teacher highlights two or three strong examples for the class.

Brief whole-class discussion comparing the funny man’s absurdist comedy with the wit characters from Indian tradition encountered earlier in the chapter — what is similar about how they use reversal, surprise and politeness to create humour?

periods.teacher_notes: This synthesis draws on the poem’s central device of inversion, the phrasal verb work in “Let us learn”, and the cross-cultural humour exploration in “Let us explore” — any class that has studied the poem’s content can participate, regardless of which specific activities they encountered. The writing task is complete within the time available: students draft and share in class, with no continuation expected afterward. The comparison in the final band is open-ended; the goal is noticing shared structural patterns (reversal, unexpected logic, the non-answer) rather than arriving at a fixed conclusion.

items.source_context: Absurdist inversions, synesthetic oxymorons, ABCB rhyme scheme, dialogue structure, repetition of ‘funny’ across six stanzas.
items.item_stem:
Read the lines on page 60 beginning “He said, Allow me to present” and answer the question below.

Which of the following best describes what the funny man actually gives the narrator, and why it is funny?

options.label: A
options.text: He gives a currant bun while announcing it as a rose, making the gift absurdly misnamed.

options.label: B
options.text: He gives a real rose, which is funny because he calls it a currant bun.

options.label: C
options.text: He gives a shoe, because the poem is entirely about wearing the wrong objects.

options.label: D
options.text: He gives nothing, and the humour lies in his empty promise.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Suggests the student reversed the object names, confusing what was said with what was done.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Indicates the student missed the stanza’s action entirely and recalled only the promised item.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Overgeneralises the shoe-and-hat inversion motif to an object not present in this stanza.

items.source_lo: Student identifies and interprets literal and inferential meaning in a poem using sustained close reading as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Absurdist inversions, synesthetic oxymorons, ABCB rhyme scheme, dialogue structure, repetition of ‘funny’ across six stanzas.
items.item_stem: The poem uses phrases such as “a funny sounding sight” and “a funny feeling sound” to describe the funny man’s actions. In two or three sentences, explain what effect these deliberately mixed-up sense words create, and what they suggest about the world the poet is building in the poem.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: The phrases mix sense words that do not logically belong together — seeing produces a sight, not a sound, and hearing produces a sound, not a feeling — creating a synesthetic oxymoron that mirrors the man’s own inverted reality. This deliberate mismatch suggests that in the funny man’s world the ordinary rules of logic and language have been turned upside-down, just as his shoe is on his head and his hats are on his feet.

items.source_lo: Student demonstrates comprehension of a spoken personal anecdote by identifying key details and sequencing events using listening as the vehicle.
items.source_context: A girl’s absent-minded mix-up: plate placed on desk, shoes in kitchen after a long study day.
items.item_stem:
Read the statements below about the girl’s anecdote and decide whether each is TRUE or FALSE. If FALSE, write the correct information in one sentence.

(1) The girl had spent the day studying at her own home before the mix-up occurred.
(2) The girl placed her plate on her desk instead of returning it to the kitchen.
(3) The girl laughed at her mistake after realising what she had done.
(4) At the end of the anecdote the girl left her shoes in the kitchen permanently.

options.text: At the end of the anecdote the girl left her shoes in the kitchen permanently.
The girl had spent the day studying at her own home before the mix-up occurred.
The girl laughed at her mistake after realising what she had done.
The girl placed her plate on her desk instead of returning it to the kitchen.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer:
1. False — she had been studying at a friend’s place, not her own home.
2. True — she walked to her room with her plate and left it on her desk.
3. True — the transcript states she could not help but laugh at herself.
4. False — she recovered her shoes from the kitchen and put them away properly.

items.source_lo: Student demonstrates comprehension of a spoken personal anecdote by identifying key details and sequencing events using listening as the vehicle.
items.source_context: A girl’s absent-minded mix-up: plate placed on desk, shoes in kitchen after a long study day.
items.item_stem: Listen to the anecdote again and fill in the table below by writing each event in its correct order of occurrence. The first event has been done for you.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1. Studied at a friend’s place. 2. Came home and removed shoes at the door. 3. Served and ate dal-chawal in the kitchen. 4. Walked to her room carrying the plate (and left it on the desk). 5. Placed shoes in the kitchen. 6. Realised the mistake and laughed, then corrected it.

items.source_lo: Student performs a scripted and an original humorous exchange with appropriate voice modulation using oral presentation as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Man-and-God joke with three voice registers; student-created joke with punchline — from the poem’s chapter.
items.item_stem: Work with a partner. Choose any three-turn humorous exchange — it may be a joke you know or one from everyday life. Read it aloud, each person playing at least one character. Use a different voice for each speaker (for example: calm narrator, excited character, quiet character). Your teacher will listen as you perform.

expected_elements: Uses a clearly different voice or tone for each character.
Speaks at a pace the audience can follow.
The punchline or twist is delivered with a brief pause for effect.
Partners take turns without interrupting each other.

items.source_lo: Student performs a scripted and an original humorous exchange with appropriate voice modulation using oral presentation as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Man-and-God joke with three voice registers; student-created joke with punchline — from the poem’s chapter.
items.item_stem: With your partner, create a short original joke that includes at least two characters and ends with a surprise or twist, similar to how the funny man’s behaviour surprises the narrator in the poem. Perform it in front of the class. After your performance, explain in one sentence what made your joke funny.

expected_elements: Joke has a clear setup, at least one exchange, and a surprise ending.
Student can name the twist or reversal that creates the humour.
Delivery is loud and clear enough for the class to hear.
Explanation connects the twist to the idea of the unexpected.

items.source_lo: Student composes an original humorous verse following a prescribed form and structure using literary writing as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Limerick form — AABBA rhyme scheme, five-line structure, unexpected final line, nonsensical content.
items.item_stem: A limerick follows the AABBA rhyme scheme and has five lines: line 1 introduces a person or place; lines 2–4 tell a silly story; line 5 gives an unexpected ending. Write a limerick about the funny man from the poem, keeping to the five-line AABBA structure and making the final line a surprise.

expected_elements: Five lines present with AABBA rhyme scheme correctly applied.
Line 1 introduces the funny man or his street.
Lines 2–4 include an absurd or silly detail from or inspired by the poem.
Line 5 delivers a surprise or unexpected ending.

items.source_lo: Student composes an original humorous verse following a prescribed form and structure using literary writing as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Limerick form — AABBA rhyme scheme, five-line structure, unexpected final line, nonsensical content.
items.item_stem: Write an original limerick about any character or place of your own invention. Your limerick must follow the AABBA rhyme scheme, use a clearly absurd or nonsensical event in lines 2–4, and end with a line that turns the reader’s expectation upside-down. After writing your limerick, add one sentence explaining the twist or absurdity you chose and why it is funny.

expected_elements: Five-line limerick with correct AABBA rhyme scheme throughout.
Lines 2–4 contain a clearly absurd or illogical event.
Line 5 subverts or reverses the expectation set up in line 1.
Explanatory sentence names the specific twist and connects it to humour.

items.item_stem: Match each phrasal verb in Column A with its correct meaning in Column B.
items.visual_stimulus:
Column A|Column B
take after|to assume control or responsibility for something
take in|to resemble a family member in looks or manner
take off|to understand or comprehend something
take over|to begin to study, practise, or do something
take up|to become successful or popular quickly

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: take after — to resemble a family member in looks or manner; take in — to understand or comprehend something; take off — to become successful or popular quickly; take over — to assume control or responsibility for something; take up — to begin to study, practise, or do something.

answer_key.right: to resemble a family member in looks or manner
to become successful or popular quickly
to assume control or responsibility for something
to begin to study, practise, or do something

items.source_context: TAKE phrasal verbs (take up, after, in, over, off); verbs look/run/put/break/call with particles; movement-verb pace scale.
items.item_stem: The funny man in the poem walks, hops and staggers through the street. Using what you know about phrasal verbs (for example: look after, run away, put off, break down, call up), write three original sentences. Each sentence must use a different phrasal verb and must describe an action that could plausibly happen on the street where the funny man walks. Underline the phrasal verb in each sentence.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Accept any three grammatically correct sentences that each use a distinct phrasal verb (from the TAKE set or the look/run/put/break/call set studied), place the action on or near the street setting of the poem, and have the phrasal verb underlined. Example: ‘A child ran away when she spotted the man hopping on his head.’

items.source_lo: Student connects the poem’s absurdist humour to broader literary and cultural traditions using interdisciplinary study as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Wit characters from Indian tradition (Tenali Rama, Birbal, Mullah Nasruddin, Betal); Sukumar Ray’s Abol Tabol; native-language nonsense poetry.
items.item_stem: Characters such as Tenali Rama, Birbal and Mullah Nasruddin are celebrated in Indian literary tradition for using wit and surprising logic to make a point. Choose ONE of these characters and write a paragraph of five to seven sentences describing a story or situation involving that character. In your paragraph, identify one way in which the character’s wit is similar to the funny man’s behaviour in the poem.

expected_elements: Names one specific character and briefly describes a story or situation.
Identifies a shared feature (e.g., reversal, unexpected logic, polite absurdity).
Refers to a specific moment in the poem to support the comparison.
Written in clear, connected sentences of appropriate length.

items.source_lo: Student connects the poem’s absurdist humour to broader literary and cultural traditions using interdisciplinary study as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Wit characters from Indian tradition (Tenali Rama, Birbal, Mullah Nasruddin, Betal); Sukumar Ray’s Abol Tabol; native-language nonsense poetry.
items.item_stem: Sukumar Ray’s Abol Tabol poems, like “A Funny Man” by Natalie Joan, use nonsense and inversion to create humour. Design a short project plan (not the project itself) in which you explain: (a) which humorous or nonsense poem from Indian literature or your own language you would explore; (b) what specific feature of absurdity or inversion you would focus on; and (c) how you would present your findings to the class — for example, a reading, a poster, or a short talk. Write your plan in a clear, organised format.

expected_elements: Names a specific poem or tradition from Indian literature or their own language.
Identifies a concrete feature of absurdity, inversion or nonsense to focus on.
Proposes a clear and feasible presentation format for the class.
Plan is written in an organised, readable structure with at least three distinct points.
